Replication materials · 34 stabilisations, 1921–2025

The data behind the paper

A descriptive tour of every series used in “Whose Dates Do Prices Obey? Fiscal Regime Change and the Anchoring of Inflation” (Gustavo Vargas, 2026; presented at the Economic Affairs Research Workshop, Vinson Centre, University of Buckingham)

Table 1 sample Intermediate Failed plans COVID UK 2022 Velocity
How to read this page. It presents the data, not the results: what each series is, where it comes from, what window the paper uses and what the raw monthly rates look like. Each episode card gives a short historical note, the dated policy event (the red dashed line; a day of 1 means only the month is dated), the census outcome label — durable, gradual, temporary, failure or in progress, coded under the protocol in the paper's appendix A — the analysis window, coverage and source, and a chart. Charts plot 100 × the monthly log change, which keeps hyperinflations on a readable scale; the card summaries convert to conventional percentages (100 × (eΔln − 1) — at low rates the two are close, at hyperinflation rates they differ enormously). Lines break where months are missing. Two episodes are deliberate reflations (United States 1933, Japan 1931): there the policy's objective was to raise the price level. The break tests and estimates live in src/estimacion/ and in the paper's appendix.

The census counts 34 stabilisation programmes launched between 1921 and 2023 (the study's universe closes in 2025), of which 31 have usable monthly data — the three without are Hungary's 1921 Hegedüs attempt (the price index begins as it died), Hungary's 1946 forint and Nicaragua 1991 (print sources only). That makes 46 episode-window series (31 price, 15 money; several episodes cut different windows from the same underlying national series), plus three daily series for the 2022 UK episode, a 19-country cross-section for the COVID inflation and two quarterly US velocity series. Hand-digitised series carry their source, page numbers, splices and known printing errata in the file headers under data/manual/; the rest load from public APIs without keys (FRED, the IMF, and the central banks of Brazil, Peru and Argentina), cached with date stamps under data/raw/.

The Table 1 sample: fifteen stabilisations with a fiscal anchor

The episodes behind the paper's main timing test (its Table 1): monthly price indices, and a monthly money series where a usable one exists — banknotes in circulation for the 1920s, the monetary base, M1, M2 or M3 later; each card names its source. 'Fiscal anchor' follows the census coding protocol (appendix A of the paper, reproduced in this repository): an executed or statutory fiscal component, coded from acts of policy, never from the inflation outcome.

Austria 1922 — League of Nations protocols durable success

Austria left the First World War with a collapsing crown and a budget financed by the printing press. The crown actually steadied in late August 1922, on the news that the League of Nations would take the reconstruction in hand; the Geneva Protocols of October formalised the package — a guaranteed foreign loan, a commissioner with authority over the budget, and a central bank barred from lending to the government, operating from January 1923. Prices peaked in September — while the note circulation went on rising for two more years.

Dated policy event: 02 Oct 1922 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1921–Jun 1924  ·  Price series: Feb 1921–Jun 1924, n = 41 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 29  ·  Exchange-rate series: n = 41
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 128.7% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 54.3%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from Sargent (1982)

Germany 1923 — Rentenmark + fiscal reform durable success

The classic hyperinflation: the occupation of the Ruhr in 1923 was met with 'passive resistance' paid for by the printing press, and by November prices were doubling in days. Passive resistance had ended on 26 September; the Rentenmark of 15 November 1923 arrived together with the fiscal reform — budget cuts and a cap on the Reichsbank's credit to the government. Stabilisation came within weeks.

Dated policy event: 15 Nov 1923 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1922–Dec 1924  ·  Price series: Feb 1922–Dec 1924, n = 35 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 35
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 29,524.8% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 597.9%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from Sargent (1982)

Hungary 1924 — League reconstruction durable success

Hungary's post-war inflation accelerated through 1923. The League of Nations reconstruction of March 1924 repeated the Austrian template — foreign loan, budget control, a new National Bank (opened in June) forbidden to finance the Treasury — and monthly inflation slowed sharply that spring.

Dated policy event: 14 Mar 1924 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jul 1921–Mar 1925  ·  Price series: Aug 1921–Mar 1925, n = 44 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 44  ·  Exchange-rate series: n = 44
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 97.9% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 16.1%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from Sargent (1982)

Belgium 1926 — Francqui stabilisation durable success

Belgium's franc slid after a failed stabilisation attempt in 1925-26 left the Treasury unable to roll its short-term debt. From July 1926 the Jaspar government — with Francqui directing the stabilisation — used emergency powers to raise taxes earmarked for debt service and consolidate the short-term debt; the legal stabilisation and the return to gold came on 25 October 1926.

Dated policy event: 16 Jul 1926 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Apr 1924–Dec 1928  ·  Price series: May 1924–Dec 1928, n = 56 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 15.1% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 5.7%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from the Federal Reserve Bulletin (FRASER)

France 1926 — Poincaré government durable success

France's franc fell through the first half of 1926 as cabinets failed to close the deficit. Poincaré's return in July 1926, with new taxes and a fund dedicated to retiring debt, turned the franc around within days; wholesale prices broke in the months that followed, and the de jure gold parity came in 1928.

Dated policy event: 23 Jul 1926 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1922–Dec 1928  ·  Price series: Feb 1922–Dec 1928, n = 83 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window  ·  Exchange-rate series: n = 83
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 13.3% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 1.6%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: NBER Macrohistory via FRED

Japan 1931 — Takahashi reflation durable successreflation

A reflation: Japan entered 1931 in deflation under the gold standard. Takahashi Korekiyo, finance minister from December 1931, took the yen off gold and ran deficits for recovery, with the Bank of Japan underwriting government bonds directly from November 1932. Prices turned up and the deflation ended.

Dated policy event: 13 Dec 1931 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1929–Dec 1936  ·  Price series: Feb 1929–Dec 1936, n = 95 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 95  ·  Exchange-rate series: n = 95
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 8.5% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: -2.0%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Shibamoto and Shizume (2014)

US 1933 — FDR reflation durable successreflation

The other reflation: over March-April 1933 Roosevelt took the United States off gold and announced deficits with the declared purpose of raising the price level (the card dates the episode to April). Prices turned upward with the announcements while broad money was still depressed from the banking crisis.

Dated policy event: 01 Apr 1933 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1929–Dec 1937  ·  Price series: Feb 1929–Dec 1937, n = 107 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 107
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 6.3% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: -1.8%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: FRED

Israel 1985 — Economic Stabilization Plan durable success

Israel's inflation passed 400 per cent a year by 1984-85 under full indexation. The Economic Stabilization Plan of July 1985 combined a large budget cut, a fixed shekel-dollar exchange rate after a step devaluation, wage-price pacts and, soon after, a law forbidding the central bank to finance the government. Within a year inflation was running at an annual rate of about 20 per cent.

Dated policy event: 01 Jul 1985 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1983–Dec 1990  ·  Price series: Feb 1983–Dec 1990, n = 95 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 95
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 26.4% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 13.3%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: FRED/OECD

Bolivia 1985 — Decree 21060 durable success

Bolivia's hyperinflation peaked in mid-1985 after years of monetised deficits. Decree 21060 of 29 August 1985 (Paz Estenssoro) closed the deficit — hydrocarbon prices became fiscal revenue, public wages were frozen, spending was rationed to cash — and unified the exchange rate, with no price freeze and no new currency. Sachs dates the halt in price rises to 9 September, within days of the decree.

Dated policy event: 29 Aug 1985 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1984–Sep 1986  ·  Price series: Feb 1984–Sep 1986, n = 32 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 182.8% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 50.2%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from Sachs (1986)

Mexico 1987 — Solidarity Pact durable success

Mexico's inflation reached about 160 per cent a year after the 1987 crash and devaluation. The Solidarity Pact of December 1987 paired fiscal adjustment with an exchange-rate anchor and economy-wide price-wage agreements; inflation fell through 1988-89 and stayed low until the 1994-95 crisis.

Dated policy event: 15 Dec 1987 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Dec 1985–Dec 1992  ·  Price series: Jan 1986–Dec 1992, n = 84 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 84
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 15.5% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 8.0%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: FRED/OECD

Poland 1990 — Balcerowicz plan durable success

Poland left communism in late 1989 amid a hyperinflationary burst after food prices were freed. The Balcerowicz plan of 1 January 1990 — fiscal discipline, an anchored złoty, hard limits on enterprise credit — itself spiked measured prices in January as administered prices were freed (79 per cent in the month); monthly inflation then fell to 4 per cent by March, though single digits annually took most of the decade.

Dated policy event: 01 Jan 1990 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1988–Dec 1994  ·  Price series: Feb 1988–Dec 1994, n = 83 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 79.4% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 26.9%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: IMF IFS via DBnomics

Peru 1990 — Fujishock durable success

Peru's hyperinflation under García accelerated through 1988-90. The 'Fujishock' of 8 August 1990 corrected public prices overnight — 84-octane petrol rose about thirty-fold — pushing the August figure to its measured peak near 400 per cent; central-bank financing ended, and inflation collapsed in the following months.

Dated policy event: 08 Aug 1990 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1988–Dec 1993  ·  Price series: Feb 1988–Dec 1993, n = 71 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 397.0% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 35.0%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Central Reserve Bank of Peru

Brazil 1994 — Real plan durable success

Brazil's fifth plan in this census's sequence arrived with an executed fiscal leg its predecessors lacked: an emergency fiscal fund alongside the URV (a transitional unit of account), with the real introduced on 1 July 1994. Monthly inflation fell from around 45 per cent to low single digits, durably.

Dated policy event: 01 Jul 1994 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1992–Dec 1997  ·  Price series: Feb 1992–Dec 1997, n = 71 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 71
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 47.4% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 42.7%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Central Bank of Brazil (SGS) + FRED

Bulgaria 1997 — Currency board durable success

Bulgaria's banking collapse and monetised deficits produced hyperinflation that peaked in February 1997. Inflation collapsed in the spring, as the caretaker government and the IMF agreed the currency board that entered into force on 1 July 1997: the lev pegged to the Deutsche Mark and central-bank credit to the government outlawed.

Dated policy event: 01 Jul 1997 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1995–Dec 2001  ·  Price series: Feb 1995–Dec 2001, n = 83 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 242.4% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 4.8%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: IMF IFS via DBnomics

Turkey 2001 — Derviş programme durable success

Turkey's crawling peg collapsed in the February 2001 crisis and the lira floated, the depreciation passing through to prices for the rest of the year. The Derviş programme announced on 14 April 2001 — a large primary-surplus target (the budget balance before interest payments), bank restructuring and legal central-bank independence, IMF-backed — brought inflation down decisively from early 2002.

Dated policy event: 14 Apr 2001 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1998–Dec 2005  ·  Price series: Feb 1998–Dec 2005, n = 95 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 95
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 10.3% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 2.8%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: FRED/OECD

Intermediate episodes, treated separately in the paper

Eleven further episodes: six temporary successes, three durable successes outside the main sample (Italy and Ecuador, the census's monetary-led cases, and Zimbabwe, whose turn falls in a measurement gap), one gradual (Chile) and one in progress (Argentina 2023). Same series construction, same descriptive view.

Poland 1924 — Grabski reform temporary success

Poland's first stabilisation: the Grabski programme of January 1924 closed the deficit with a property tax and no foreign loan; the Bank Polski opened and the złoty entered circulation in April. The hyperinflation stopped — but the budget slipped in 1925, the złoty fell, and a 'second inflation' forced a new stabilisation in 1926-27.

Dated policy event: 11 Jan 1924 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1921–Apr 1925  ·  Price series: Feb 1921–Apr 1924, n = 39 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 51  ·  Exchange-rate series: n = 49
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 275.0% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 90.1%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from Sargent (1982)

Italy 1947 — Einaudi squeeze durable success

Italy's post-war inflation was broken by a monetary act: Einaudi's credit squeeze of August-September 1947 (higher reserve requirements, credit restriction), with the fiscal consolidation and Marshall aid arriving in its wake. The census codes it as a monetary-led stabilisation.

Dated policy event: 30 Sep 1947 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1947–Sep 1949  ·  Price series: Feb 1947–Sep 1949, n = 32 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 14.8% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 7.4%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from the Federal Reserve Bulletin (FRASER)

Chile 1975 — Cauas adjustment gradual success

Chile's inflation ran in the hundreds of per cent after 1973. The Cauas adjustment of April 1975 intensified a fiscal correction already under way; inflation declined over years rather than months — a gradual disinflation, with contract indexation the standard explanation for its slowness.

Dated policy event: 24 Apr 1975 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1974–Dec 1979  ·  Price series: Feb 1974–Dec 1979, n = 71 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 24.5% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 15.2%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: FRED/OECD

Argentina Austral 1985 — Austral plan temporary success

Argentina's Austral plan of 14 June 1985 froze prices and wages, created the austral and promised an end to money-financed deficits. Inflation stayed low for about eighteen months; as the fiscal promise eroded through 1987-88 it returned, and the economy slid into the 1989 hyperinflation.

Dated policy event: 14 Jun 1985 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jun 1983–Jul 1988  ·  Price series: Jul 1983–Jul 1988, n = 61 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 32.3% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 22.1%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: CPI of Mendoza province (DEIE, via datos.gob.ar)

Argentina Convertibility 1991 — Convertibility temporary success

Convertibility, April 1991: Cavallo fixed the exchange rate by law — 10,000 australes per US dollar, with the peso replacing the austral at one-to-one with the dollar in January 1992 — and turned the central bank into a near currency board. Annual inflation reached single digits by 1993 and hovered near zero for the rest of the decade, until the regime collapsed into default and devaluation in 2001-02.

Dated policy event: 01 Apr 1991 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Apr 1990–Dec 1996  ·  Price series: May 1990–Dec 1996, n = 80 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 26.3% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 7.4%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: CPI of Mendoza province (DEIE, via datos.gob.ar)

Yugoslavia 1994 — Avramović programme temporary success

Yugoslavia's 1993-94 hyperinflation peaked at an official 313 million per cent a month. The Avramović programme of 24 January 1994 introduced a new dinar pegged to the Deutsche Mark with a promise of no monetary financing; prices stopped within a week (February's monthly average still shows carry-over), and the stabilisation eroded from late 1995 as the fiscal side gave way — after this card's window, which ends in December 1994.

Dated policy event: 24 Jan 1994 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1992–Dec 1994  ·  Price series: Feb 1992–Dec 1994, n = 35 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 313,563,558.0% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 1,888.1%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Digitised from Bogetić et al. (2022)

Ukraine 1994 — Kuchma stabilisation temporary success

Ukraine's post-Soviet inflation peaked in 1993. Kuchma's IMF-backed package of October 1994 liberalised prices (spiking the measured rate that autumn), unified the exchange rate and began a gradual — and incomplete — fiscal adjustment; inflation fell from about 400 per cent in 1994 to 10 per cent by 1997 (December on December), before the 1998 Russian crisis forced a relapse, beyond this card's window.

Dated policy event: 11 Oct 1994 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Feb 1992–May 1998  ·  Price series: Mar 1992–May 1998, n = 75 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 90.8% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 4.5%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: IMF IFS via DBnomics

Russia 1995 — Exchange-rate corridor temporary success

Russia's stabilisation of July 1995 anchored the rouble in an exchange-rate corridor and moved deficit financing from the printing press to the bond market. Inflation fell steadily until the sovereign default and devaluation of August 1998 undid it; the window here ends just before.

Dated policy event: 06 Jul 1995 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1993–May 1998  ·  Price series: Feb 1993–May 1998, n = 64 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 26.0% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 8.7%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: FRED/OECD

Ecuador 2000 — Dollarisation durable success

Ecuador announced dollarisation on 9 January 2000, in the middle of a banking crisis and a collapsing sucre, and implemented it over the year — a complete renunciation of the printing press, with only a weak fiscal component. Inflation fell slowly, reaching single digits (year on year) only in 2002.

Dated policy event: 09 Jan 2000 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 1997–Dec 2004  ·  Price series: Feb 1997–Dec 2004, n = 95 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 14.3% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 3.6%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: IMF IFS via DBnomics

Zimbabwe 2009 — Dollarisation durable success

Zimbabwe's hyperinflation — among the worst ever measured — ended when the Zimbabwe dollar ceased to trade in late 2008. The multicurrency regime authorised over January-February 2009 and the cash budget adopted from March ('we eat what we kill', in finance minister Biti's phrase) formalised a stop the market had already made; prices then stayed stable for a decade, until a local currency returned in 2019.

Dated policy event: 13 Feb 2009 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Mar 2007–Dec 2012  ·  Price series: Apr 2007–Dec 2012, n = 67 monthly rates (2 months missing inside the range; the line breaks there)  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 79,600,000,000.0% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 2,936,735.2%/m (n = 4)  ·  Source: Hanke and Kwok (2009) + IMF IFS

Argentina 2023 — Milei adjustment in progress

The census's live entry: Milei's adjustment of 12 December 2023 devalued the peso and anchored itself to an explicit zero-deficit rule — in 2024 the national public sector posted its first full-year overall (cash) surplus since 2010. Monthly inflation fell from 25 per cent in the month of the announcement to about 2 per cent by late 2025.

Dated policy event: 12 Dec 2023 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jan 2021–Sep 2026  ·  Price series: Feb 2021–Aug 2026, n = 67 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 68
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 25.5% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 10.4%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: BCRA + INDEC (datos.gob.ar)

The failed plans

The five failures with monthly data — three plans with no credible fiscal component (Cruzado, Verão, Primavera) plus Bresser and Collor, whose announced adjustments were not delivered. A sixth census failure, Hungary's 1921 Hegedüs attempt, predates the country's price index. These episodes serve as the comparison group in the paper's durability exercise.

Brazil Cruzado 1986 — Cruzado plan failure

The Cruzado plan of February 1986 froze prices and wages and created the cruzado, with no fiscal adjustment behind it. End-of-month M1 rose about 64 per cent in March 1986 alone (≈49 in the chart's log units) while measured inflation sat near zero under the freeze; the freeze crumbled and inflation returned within the year.

Dated policy event: 28 Feb 1986 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Mar 1984–May 1987  ·  Price series: Apr 1984–May 1987, n = 38 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 38
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 21.5% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 13.0%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Central Bank of Brazil (SGS)

Brazil Bresser 1987 — Bresser plan failure

The Bresser plan of June 1987 repeated the freeze with an announced fiscal adjustment that was not delivered. By mid-1988 monthly inflation was back above 20 per cent, around its pre-plan rate.

Dated policy event: 12 Jun 1987 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Apr 1986–Dec 1988  ·  Price series: May 1986–Dec 1988, n = 32 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 32
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 28.7% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 14.8%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Central Bank of Brazil (SGS)

Argentina Primavera 1988 — Primavera plan failure

Argentina's Primavera plan of August 1988 combined price agreements and a managed crawl (a pre-announced slow devaluation), again without a fiscal leg. The exchange-rate arrangement collapsed in February 1989, and inflation surged into hyperinflation over May-July 1989.

Dated policy event: 03 Aug 1988 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Sep 1986–Jun 1989  ·  Price series: Oct 1986–Jun 1989, n = 33 monthly rates  ·  Money series: none usable for this window
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 101.5% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 15.4%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: CPI of Mendoza province (DEIE, via datos.gob.ar)

Brazil Verão 1989 — Verão plan failure

The Verão plan of January 1989 created the cruzado novo and froze prices once more; its announced fiscal measures were abandoned. Inflation accelerated again through 1989, reaching hyperinflation in early 1990, beyond this card's window.

Dated policy event: 15 Jan 1989 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Jul 1987–Feb 1990  ·  Price series: Aug 1987–Feb 1990, n = 31 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 31
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 75.7% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 26.5%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Central Bank of Brazil (SGS)

Brazil Collor 1990 — Collor plan failure

The Collor plan of March 1990 sequestered most of the financial system's liquid assets — yet narrow money, converted at the frozen rate, actually rose (about 124 per cent in March); the plotted M1 does not measure the frozen broad assets. Inflation was back around 20 per cent a month by early 1991.

Dated policy event: 16 Mar 1990 (dashed red)
Analysis window: Feb 1989–Dec 1991  ·  Price series: Mar 1989–Dec 1991, n = 34 monthly rates  ·  Money series: n = 34
Peak monthly inflation in this window: 82.4% (conventional)  ·  Median of the six months before the reform month: 49.6%/m (n = 6)  ·  Source: Central Bank of Brazil (SGS)

The COVID cross-section (19 countries)

One row per country. Cumulative inflation is consumer-price inflation compounded over 2020–23 (Eurostat/OECD/World Bank). The fiscal impulse is the IMF Fiscal Monitor's above-the-line COVID measure — additional spending plus forgone revenue, per cent of GDP, October 2021 vintage. Debt and average maturity are end-2019 values (national debt offices, the ECB and IMF WEO); the scatter's horizontal axis divides the impulse by debt-to-GDP (as a fraction) times maturity in years, a scaled indicator rather than a forecast. Maturity definitions are not perfectly homogeneous across countries. The scatter shows the data as used; estimates are in the paper, not here.

The 2022 UK episode (daily data)

1 September to 31 October 2022: the pound against the dollar (FRED DEXUSUK) and the ten-year nominal and real zero-coupon yields on gilts — UK government bonds — from the Bank of England's database (IUDMNZC and IUDMRZC; the real yield is derived from index-linked gilts, not from realised inflation). The file holds 43 dated rows across both calendars: GBP/USD n = 41, nominal gilt n = 42, real gilt n = 42. Dotted lines: the 'mini-budget' of unfunded tax cuts (23 September), the Bank of England's temporary gilt purchases (28 September) and the withdrawal of the package (17 October).

US velocity series

Velocity is nominal GDP divided by a money measure. Left: M2 velocity from FRED (M2V), 1959Q1–2025Q4, n = 268 quarters. Right: nominal GDP divided by the Center for Financial Stability's Divisia M4 — a broad aggregate that weights assets by their monetary services — which is an index (January 1967 = 100), so the level of this ratio has an arbitrary scale and only its movements are informative; 1967Q1–2025Q4, n = 236. The paper's section 7 runs the stationarity battery on exactly these two series.

Generated on 18 October 2026 by src/datos_descriptivos.py from this repository's data (the UK panel reads src/estimacion/out/truss_event_study.csv, produced by src/estimacion/truss.py; API series load from the dated caches in data/raw/, so regenerating on a later date may fetch newer vintages) · Replication repository · Code and compilation MIT-licensed; underlying series remain subject to their sources' terms.
